analysis.one_liner: Abolishes the Environmental Protection Agency entirely.
analysis.headline: The bill to abolish the EPA never got a hearing or a vote; the agency still exists and its powers were not transferred to any other body.
analysis.plain_summary: This one-page bill would have shut down the Environmental Protection Agency — the federal agency that enforces clean air and clean water laws, regulates pesticides and toxic chemicals, and cleans up hazardous waste sites — on December 31, 2018. It named no replacement agency and transferred none of the EPA's duties. The bill was sent to four House committees, never received a hearing or a vote, and died when that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Industries that face EPA enforcement — fossil fuel producers, chemical manufacturers, mines, and large industrial facilities — would no longer face a federal regulator setting emission limits, testing chemicals, or penalizing violations. Individual states would gain discretion over environmental rules within their borders.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Industrial polluters and their trade groups

how_it_helps.text: It would eliminate a federal regulator that imposes compliance costs on oil, gas, chemical, mining, and manufacturing companies.
It would remove the agency that sets and enforces national limits on air and water pollution, pesticide use, and toxic waste cleanup.

analysis.who_pays: Everyone who breathes air or drinks water — the cost of shutting down federal environmental enforcement falls on the public, along with the roughly 14,000 EPA employees who would lose their jobs and the states left to handle pollution alone without federal funding or expertise.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public and state environmental agencies

drawbacks.text: The bill proposes no replacement: it simply ends the agency, leaving no federal body to enforce clean-air and clean-water laws or evaluate chemical safety after December 31, 2018.
Terminating the EPA would leave states to police interstate pollution on their own, even though pollution crossing state lines is a core reason a federal agency exists.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs — dirtier air and water, no federal cop on environmental enforcement, and health risks borne disproportionately by people living near pollution sources — far outweighed any benefit, which was limited to savings and reduced paperwork for the industries and states the EPA regulates. The bill also offered no plan for maintaining federal environmental standards, and it never received even a committee vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to four House committees, then to subcommittees, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Matt Gaetz introduced H.R. 861 on February 3, 2017, with a single sentence of substance: the Environmental Protection Agency would terminate on December 31, 2018.
The House referred it to four committees — Energy and Commerce, Agriculture, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Science, Space, and Technology — none of which acted on it.

It was passed down to subcommittees (the Subcommittee on Economic Development, Public Buildings and Emergency Management, and the Subcommittee on Environment) and stayed there for the rest of the 115th Congress, which ended January 3, 2019.
Seven Republican representatives cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did, and no vote was ever taken.
The Environmental Protection Agency still exists and was not abolished.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Polluting industries benefited from the outcome: the EPA remains intact and its regulations remain in force, but a bill to eliminate them never had to survive public scrutiny or a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Polluting industries, which faced no repeal fight

for.name: Rep. Matt Gaetz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to terminate the EPA and recruited original cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: All seven cosponsors were Republicans and the sponsor was a Republican; no Democrat supported it, and the bill never advanced far enough for a recorded vote.

industries.industry: Polluting industries (fossil fuels, chemicals, mining, manufacturing)
industries.note: Abolishing the EPA would end federal enforcement of air, water, and toxic-waste rules, cutting compliance costs but exposing nearby residents to more pollution.
States would be left to handle environmental protection alone, with no federal backstop, funding, or scientific support, and no way to police pollution coming from other states.
